opus-5.5.text:
Well, the simplest form of inference-time scaling is what people were already doing: you take an autoregressive LLM, you sample many candidate answers, and then you pick one, either by majority vote or by having some verifier, sometimes another LLM, pick the best. That's essentially generate-and-test. It helps a bit, but if the generator's distribution doesn't have the right answer with reasonable probability, more sampling doesn't buy you much. And we saw in our own experiments, on things like Blocksworld planning problems, that these approaches plateau pretty quickly.

What o1 does seems qualitatively different. First, the performance improvements on our planning benchmarks, especially on the obfuscated "Mystery Blocksworld" versions where the LLMs of the previous generation basically fell to near zero, were too large to be explained by just sampling more and voting. Second, the behavior and cost profile tell you something. You're paying for these "reasoning tokens" that you don't get to see, and the amount of those tokens varies with the problem. That suggests the model has been trained to *do* something with that intermediate computation, not just ramble.

My best guess, and I want to be clear it's a guess because OpenAI hasn't told us, is that it's something like AlphaGo-style reinforcement learning applied to the space of chain-of-thought. Think of the intermediate tokens as pseudo-actions. You generate lots of traces, on problems where you can check the answer, like math and code, and those that lead to correct solutions give you a reward signal. Then you learn something like a Q-function, how good is it to emit this piece of "thought" in this state, and you use that to fine-tune the base model. So at inference time it's not just blind sampling; it's sampling guided by a policy that was shaped by RL over these reasoning traces. Whether there's also some explicit search, rollouts, at inference time, that's possible too.

That's why I've started calling it a "large reasoning model" rather than an LLM. It's not just doing approximate retrieval in the autoregressive sense anymore; there's a learned, post-trained procedure on top. But I'd also caution, it's still not giving you guarantees. It does better, but it still makes mistakes, it can't always say "this problem is unsolvable," and it's quite expensive. So it's more sophisticated, yes, but it's not suddenly a sound reasoner. You still want external verifiers in the loop, which is the LLM-Modulo argument we've been making.

r001.rationale: The response says generate-and-test approaches plateau and that O1's large benchmark gains are too large to be explained by sampling and voting alone.

r002.rationale: It describes O1 as expensive but does not compare the business cost of online inference with pretraining.

r003.rationale: It discusses sampling many candidates as a general method but does not state that such methods use more inference time than O1.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, look, the first thing I should say is that nobody outside OpenAI actually knows what o1 is doing, so everything I say is informed speculation. But I think the speculation can be reasonably well grounded.

The simplest story people tell is that o1 is just "let the model think longer" — you sample more chains of thought, maybe do best-of-n with a verifier, maybe do some tree search over partial solutions at inference time. And that's the kind of thing people were already doing with GPT-4, right? Self-consistency, tree of thoughts, all of that. The problem is that those approaches give you fairly modest improvements, and they tend to plateau quickly. If that were all o1 was, I don't think you'd see the kind of jumps on, say, AIME or competition math that they're reporting. We had those inference-time tricks for two years, and they didn't give anybody o1.

The second reason is the training story they themselves hint at. They talk about reinforcement learning on reasoning, and they show these plots where performance scales with both train-time compute and test-time compute. That train-time axis is the tell. If you're only doing inference-time scaling, there's nothing to train — you'd just wrap a search loop around an existing model. The fact that they've invested heavily in RL suggests they're generating lots of chains of thought, checking which ones lead to correct answers in domains where you can verify — math, code — and then using that signal to change the model's weights. So the model is being taught, in effect, what kinds of intermediate moves tend to pay off. That's closer to what AlphaGo did with its policy network than to just running more rollouts.

And then the third thing — and this is the one I find most interesting from a planning perspective — is that the model is producing what look like very long, meandering traces that include backtracking, "wait, let me reconsider," checking its own work. You don't get that behavior spontaneously from a standard autoregressive LLM trained on web text. Humans don't typically write out their dead ends. So that behavior has to have been induced somehow, either by synthetic trace data or by the RL process rewarding traces that eventually succeed. Either way, that's a learned search procedure being compiled into the model, not search being bolted on at inference time.

Now, I want to be careful here, because I've been quite critical of the claim that LLMs "reason" in any principled sense, and I still am. What I think o1 is, is an LLM that has internalized something like a search policy — it's learned heuristics for what to try next in the kinds of problems it was trained on. That's genuinely more than just inference-time scaling. But it's also not a sound reasoner. It doesn't have a verifier in the loop at inference time that guarantees correctness; the verification happened during training, and what got distilled into the model is a tendency, not a guarantee. So you still see it make confident mistakes, and you still see the performance fall off outside the distribution of problems it was trained on, which is exactly what you'd expect if it's learned heuristics rather than learned an algorithm.

So my short answer is: the behavioral evidence — the magnitude of the gains, the dependence on train-time compute, and the shape of the reasoning traces — all point to something that was learned into the model, not something that's merely being done to the model at inference time. Whether you want to call that "reasoning" is a separate argument, and I suspect we'll get to that.

r001.rationale: It says general inference-time approaches gave only modest gains and plateaued, and argues they do not explain the reported O1 results on AIME and competition math.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the business cost of online inference with pretraining.

r003.rationale: It does not state that general inference-time-scaling methods use more inference time than O1.

astra-6.text:
Well, we don’t actually know what O1 is doing internally, so I would separate the observation from the explanation. The observation is that giving it more time appears to improve its performance on certain reasoning tasks. But “more inference-time compute” doesn’t, by itself, explain how that compute is being used.

You could sample more answers, you could generate longer chains of thought, or you could explore alternatives and evaluate them. Those are quite different procedures. Simply letting a model talk longer doesn’t guarantee that it will recognize a mistake or move toward a correct answer.

So my suspicion is that there is something learned about how to use that additional computation—how to pursue intermediate steps, reconsider them, and select a promising continuation. That needn’t mean there is an explicit symbolic planner hidden inside. It could be a strategy learned through training. But the interesting part is the mechanism that makes extra computation useful, not merely the fact that you spent more computation. And without details of the system, I would keep that as a hypothesis.

r001.rationale: The response says extra time appears to improve performance on certain tasks, but does not state that general inference-time scaling has failed to match O1’s accuracy.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the business cost of online inference with pretraining.

r003.rationale: The response lists possible ways to spend more inference compute but does not say any use more time than O1.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, inference-time scaling tells you that you're spending more computation at test time; it doesn't tell you what you're doing with that computation. You could generate a hundred answers and take a majority vote. But you could also explore different approaches, evaluate intermediate steps, backtrack, and allocate more effort to promising branches. Those are very different mechanisms, even if both use more tokens.

My suspicion is that o1 has learned something about how to use that additional computation—when to reconsider an approach, for example—rather than simply producing longer answers. Reinforcement learning could be an important part of that. But we should distinguish that hypothesis from knowing its internal architecture. The observed improvement doesn't, by itself, establish that there's an explicit search procedure or a separate verifier inside.

And the crucial question for me is still: what provides the feedback? Generating more possibilities is useful, but reliably recognizing which possibility is correct is a separate problem. More computation doesn't automatically solve that.
